name: REHAU — “Recycle for Good” CSR pilot
description: Team project on a real company case: REHAU Window Solutions asked how to design a CSR pilot for 2025–2027 that overcomes consumer skepticism about recycled PVC in South-East Europe. Our answer: collect old PVC from residents and turn it into window renovations for rural schools in Serbia.
context: A real business case, not a simulation: REHAU Window Solutions, part of the German REHAU group, wrote it for the Belgrade Business International Case Competition (BBICC 2024). NEOMA used it in January 2026 in its International Case Study Competition course, where teams work like a consulting firm and pitch their recommendation as a client presentation.

Group 4 was a team of six: Antoine Smolar, Lucas Soler, Nathan Souillard, Gabriel Thillay, QingYun Tung and Albert Vallée-Duval. The result is a team effort; I presented the environment analysis and the solution. The original case document belongs to REHAU and the competition, so only our own deck is shown here.

work.title: The problem
work.text: REHAU had the credentials but not the hearts. Its sustainability work was real, yet invisible or unconvincing to the people who actually buy windows.
points: A strong position: REHAU Window Solutions has the strongest brand awareness in its sector in Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and North Macedonia, 25 years in Serbia and a new showroom in Belgrade.
A solid circular-economy record: the EcoPuls label for recycled profiles, CO2 emissions cut by 68% between 2018 and 2022, an EcoVadis gold medal.
But a consumer bias: in South-East Europe, recycled products are seen as “good for the planet” but of lower quality, and the circular economy is poorly understood.
An emotional gap: REHAU's success is mostly B2B, with little emotional bond with end users, and competitors could claim the sustainability topic first.
The question set: how can REHAU design a CSR pilot for 2025–2027 that overcomes this skepticism and makes it the emotional leader in sustainability, with a realistic plan, budget and risks?

work.title: Our recommendation
work.text: “Recycle for Good”: a 2-year pilot in Serbia where residents bring old PVC, REHAU recycles it into new windows, and every set amount collected pays for the thermal renovation of a rural school.
points: The Novak Djokovic Foundation as partner, for reach and credibility.
€410,000 invested for €2.25M of projected incremental revenue over 24 months.
Recovered PVC replaces part of the virgin, oil-based raw material.

work.title: My part
work.text: I worked on and presented the environment analysis (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats, competition) and the solution itself, the PVC collection loop.

work.title: Methods
work.text: SCQA framing, a MECE issue tree, PESTEL, SWOT, competitor mapping, a target persona, a phased roadmap, a scored risk matrix and a cost and revenue model.

text: Group 4: Antoine Smolar, Lucas Soler, Nathan Souillard, Gabriel Thillay, QingYun Tung and Albert Vallée-Duval.
Question: how can REHAU design a CSR pilot (2025–2027) that overcomes consumer skepticism and positions the brand as the undisputed emotional leader in sustainability?

transcript.title: Executive summary
text: REHAU secures emotional leadership by turning PVC waste into a return on investment through the “Recycle for Good” initiative.
The complication: only 14% of Serbian schools are well insulated, while citizens in the region remain deeply skeptical of the quality of recycled materials.
The solution: a 2-year, high-visibility pilot in Serbia with the Novak Djokovic Foundation, to give tangible “proof of comfort”.
Financial impact: a €410,000 strategic investment driving €2.25M of incremental revenue over 24 months.
Strategic alignment: directly supports REHAU’s 2025 targets of a 30% CO2 reduction and 15% recycled material.

transcript.title: Environment analysis (presented by Antoine Smolar)
text: Strengths: 30 years of experience in closed-loop circular economy, a 75-year history of family-owned innovation, and an EcoVadis gold medal.
Weaknesses: women hold 15% of leadership roles, and the strategy must be adapted across nine countries with different cultures and economies.
Threat: a deep-rooted consumer bias in South-East Europe against products made from recycled materials, seen as inferior.
Opportunity: many government and non-profit stakeholders (Novak Djokovic Foundation, UNICEF…) available for CSR collaborations that validate the quality message.

Competition: premium players (Schüco, Internorm, Geberit) compete on technical performance, others (VEKA, aluplast, Deceuninck) on price; REHAU can be the only one linking EcoPuls quality with a tangible social impact in Serbia.

transcript.title: The solution: “Recycle for Good” (presented by Antoine Smolar)
text: A PVC collection campaign: residents bring old PVC voluntarily, the material is recycled into new windows, and every X tonnes collected pays for the thermal renovation of a rural school with REHAU windows.

transcript.title: Strategic alliance: the Novak Djokovic Foundation
text: Partnering with the Foundation provides the “quality seal” and the viral reach needed to convert the market.
Emotional hook: Novak Djokovic’s social media reach mobilises citizens for the “Recycle for Good” challenge.
Credibility: the Foundation acts as a trusted validator, showing skeptical families that recycled can mean premium quality.
Precision targeting: the Foundation’s education data helps select the rural schools with the most critical insulation needs.

transcript.title: Implementation strategy
text: A 24-month roadmap in four phases.

head: Phase
Key activities
Owner
rows: Sign the Novak Djokovic Foundation partnership and hire a lead; contract local waste firms.
Kick-off at the Belgrade showroom; install collection hubs and a live digital tracker.
Renovate 5 rural schools with EcoPuls windows; certify 20 unemployed candidates.
Release the “Generation Loop” before/after video; audit results and prepare a rollout to Croatia.

transcript.title: The risks
text: Risks scored by probability × impact (1 to 5 each).

head: Risk
Probability
Impact
Score
Mitigation
rows: “Healthy learning environments” pitch, backup NGO partners, early legal review.
Hub design and graphics that keep general waste out, plus a sorting step.
Novak Djokovic’s social reach, officials and influencers at launch, an incentive for participants.
Partnerships with local construction firms, stipend or transport allowance.
Plug collection into existing waste streams, focus on high-volume construction waste.

transcript.title: Financials
text: Pillar 1, commercial acceleration and acquisition: new customers won by a viral campaign proving the quality of recycled products, and institutions (ministries, foundations) as brand ambassadors with long-term B2B contracts.

Pillar 2, raw material savings: the PVC collected to trigger each renovation is sized to leave a surplus of recycled PVC; reusing it cuts energy use in production, and free recovered material replaces volatile, oil-based virgin PVC in the cost of goods sold.

transcript.title: Estimation
text: Pillar 1, brand awareness: +10–15% in year one, +15–20% in year two.
Pillar 2: −45% energy consumption and a COGS reduction of €500 per tonne.

transcript.title: Costs and projected revenue
text: Investment of €410,000 over 24 months for €2.25M of projected incremental revenue.

head: Item

Assumption

50 PVC collection hubs and a 2-year transport contract with local waste firms.

+10% on a €45M turnover, from B2B developers favouring certified sustainable profiles.

transcript.title: SCQA framework
text: Situation: REHAU Window Solutions has the strongest brand awareness in key South-East Europe markets, a circular economy record (EcoPuls label, CO2 emissions cut by 68% between 2018 and 2022) and 25 years in Serbia, with a new showroom in Belgrade.
Complication: citizens misunderstand the circular economy and see recycled products as inferior; B2B success lacks an emotional bond with end users; competitors could claim the topic first.
Question: how can REHAU design a CSR pilot (2025–2027) that overcomes consumer skepticism and makes it the emotional leader in sustainability?
Answer: a high-visibility renovation pilot in Serbia or Croatia, a viral mechanism involving citizens, and alliances with ministries and non-profits to validate “recycled = quality”.

transcript.title: MECE issue tree
text: Why is REHAU’s CSR performance not recognised despite strong initiatives? Five branches:
Lack of communication on CSR actions (benefits not understood, efforts unknown).
Existing but ineffective action (no impact, or effective but not satisfying the public).
Errors affecting today’s reputation (a potential historical scandal, greenwashing accusations).
CSR not aligned with public priorities (little “social” visibility in the ESG mix, technical circularity versus emotional sustainability).
Comparison with more visible CSR actors (ESG rankings and certifications, the halo effect of consumer brands).

transcript.title: PESTEL analysis (1/2)
text: Political: Serbia (outside the EU) has run a circular economy development programme since 2022; Croatia, Hungary, Slovenia and Greece (EU) face the 2026 Circular Economy Act and strict rules on waste, water and carbon.

Economic: construction services in Serbia grow 3.8% a year (€1.4 billion by 2028); the EU provides €17.5 billion for energy-saving technologies; Croatia grew 4.8% in 2025 and expects 2.5% in 2026, with €40 million earmarked for energy renovation.
Social: citizens see recycled products as good for the planet but fear lower quality; women account for 68% of sorting-related and 61% of consumption-related behaviours.

transcript.title: PESTEL analysis (2/2)
text: Technological: an intense innovation race (about 100 patents a year from industry leaders), demand for smart integrated products, digitised services, and the ARTEVO standard for the 2026 “zero emissions” requirements.
Environmental: Croatia’s national climate plan targets the construction sector, one of the region’s largest CO2 emitters, while landfill capacity is saturated.
Legal: UN Global Compact obligations, stricter rules in the EU than in Serbia, and ISO 14000 certification in Croatia.

transcript.title: Competitor analysis
text: Price/quality map: Schüco, Internorm, Geberit and REHAU in the high price, high quality corner; VEKA mid-range; aluplast, Profine, Deceuninck, Salamander and Saint-Gobain at lower price points.

transcript.title: Target persona: Ana Petrović
text: 29, marketing specialist, urban apartment owner, middle to upper class.
Goal: an energy-efficient, modern renovation, lower utility bills and “proof of comfort”.
Behaviour: researches deeply online and trusts experts over ads; practical, value-driven, cautious.
Pain points: high upfront cost compared with cheaper competitors, and doubts that recycled PVC is durable.
Quote: “I want a sustainable, modern home that saves money, but I refuse to sacrifice quality for it.”

transcript.title: SWOT analysis
text: Strengths: strongest brand awareness in Serbia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and North Macedonia; technical expertise; EcoVadis gold medal.
Weaknesses: 15% of leadership roles held by women; nine countries with different contexts.
Opportunities: first integrated showroom in Belgrade; partners such as UNDP and GIZ; growing EU and national focus on energy efficiency.
Threats: competitors winning segments with direct-to-consumer or lower prices; regional bias against recycled products; economies prioritising cost over the environment.

transcript.title: Detailed implementation plan
text: Phase I, strategic setup (months 1–4), REHAU SEE management and legal: sign the Foundation partnership, appoint the team, contract local logistics.
Phase II, launch and collection (months 5–8), marketing and operations: kick-off at the Belgrade showroom, PVC hubs at partner retailers, a public “total PVC collected” tracker.
Phase III, “good deeds” execution (months 9–18), project managers and HR: replace windows in Serbian schools with EcoPuls profiles, launch a 6-month job training for 20 unemployed people.
Phase IV, validation and regional transfer (months 19–24), regional team and PR: measure CO2 reductions, release the “Generation Loop” content.

transcript.title: Detailed risk matrix
text: Full version of the risk table, with the mitigation measures in detail (backup partners such as UNICEF Serbia, hubs with slot shapes that keep trash bags out, a launch lottery, guaranteed job interviews for trainees, collection through municipal waste streams).

transcript.title: Use of AI
text: We used Perplexity to find some sources and do research, and Gemini to structure some paragraphs; everything was reviewed by us.

transcript.title: Bibliography
text: Sources on school energy performance in Serbia and Croatia (MDPI studies, UNICEF Serbia, EU PRO, EBRD, World Bank), Balkan energy efficiency, and consumer research on green marketing and recycled products.

name: SIRTOM — Shared composters launch campaign
description: Communication campaign for the launch of shared composters across a public waste authority's territory, produced by an agency. I took part in the brief and the decisions; my proposal to lead with the financial impact was not kept, but the final campaign builds on a close idea: the value we throw away.
context: Since 1 January 2024, French law (the AGEC anti-waste law) requires bio-waste from households to be sorted at source, and it is up to local authorities to provide the solution. If residents do not sort, the authority bears the consequences and the cost. To help residents do it, SIRTOM de la région Flers-Condé launched shared composters across its territory, in Normandy, and needed a campaign to announce them.

The campaign was designed and produced by an external agency, not by me. During my internship I took part in the decisions on what to brief the agency on, how to answer its proposals and what to ask for.

work.title: My proposal: talk money, not ecology
work.text: I suggested leading with the financial side: the real savings composting brings to the authority, which directly limits increases in the waste collection tax paid by residents.
points: My reading of the audience: the area was not very receptive to environmental messages, and a genuine ecology awareness campaign would need far more time and budget.
So the message had to speak to residents' immediate, practical concerns.

work.title: What was decided: the value we throw away
work.text: The direct financial argument was not kept. The final campaign stays on the same ground, though: food scraps as something valuable that gets wasted, rather than an environmental duty.
points: The tagline: “Your food scraps have real value. Don’t waste it: compost.”

The headline plays on French slang for money: “blé, oseille, radis, avoine, patates” are crops, and most of them also mean cash. Variants follow the same idea: “Balance le blé !”, “Par ici l’oseille !”, “Donne-moi des patates !”.
The brochure backs it with figures: food and green waste make up more than 30% of household bins, about 4,000 tonnes a year on the territory, and collecting and treating them costs more every year.

work.title: A compost wheel for children
work.text: A rotating cardboard disc shows, item by item, what can go in the composter, in moderation or not at all. The aim was assumed: make it playful enough to intrigue children.
points: Short term: children push their household to start composting.
Long term: they learn the habit very young, a slow but lasting investment in awareness.

work.title: Working with the agency
work.text: I took part in the back-and-forth with the agency: reviewing its proposals, deciding on the answers and on the requests to send back.

work.title: Where the campaign ran
work.text: One visual line, declined across every touchpoint.
points: Posters (main visual and three variants) and wind flags for events.
A composter-shaped flyer with a QR code to the authority's website.
A brochure explaining why and how to compost.
Tote bags, the compost wheel, SIRTOM's social media and the livery of the waste collection trucks.
